summary: Describes the frame format for sending IPv6 packets over IEEE 1394 networks, and how to form link-local and stateless autoconfigured IPv6 addresses on them.

plainLanguage.summary: IEEE 1394 is the serial bus that was used to connect cameras, computers and audio equipment. This document explains how IPv6 traffic is carried over it, and how a computer on that bus works out its own IPv6 address from the identifier built into its hardware.

subtitle: How IPv6 packets are carried over IEEE 1394, and how addresses are formed on that bus.

tldr.problem: IEEE 1394 is a high performance serial bus that was used for audio and video equipment and for personal computers. It has its own packet formats and its own notion of a node identifier, so IPv6 needs to be told how to run over it.
tldr.mechanism: The document reuses the encapsulation and fragmentation already defined for IPv4 over 1394, sets the ether type for IPv6 to 0x86dd and the default MTU to 1500 octets, and defines how the interface identifier and link-local address are formed from the node's built-in EUI-64 identifier.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3146 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 8064, which recommends against embedding stable link-layer addresses in IPv6 interface identifiers.

today: RFC 3146 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It was later updated by RFC 8064, which recommends against embedding stable link-layer addresses in IPv6 interface identifiers, so the two should be read together.

sections.title: What This Document Covers
sections.content: This document describes the frame format for transmission of IPv6 packets and the method of forming IPv6 link-local addresses and statelessly autoconfigured addresses on IEEE 1394 networks. It also describes the content of the Source/Target Link-layer Address option used in Neighbor Discovery when the messages are transmitted on an IEEE 1394 network.
sections.plainLanguage: The document covers three things: how an IPv6 packet is put into a 1394 packet, how the computer works out its own IPv6 address, and how neighbour discovery messages carry the hardware identifier.

sections.title: What an IPv6-Capable Node Must Provide
sections.content:
An IPv6-capable node MUST fulfil several minimum requirements. It MUST implement configuration ROM in the general format specified by ISO/IEC 13213:1994, and MUST implement the bus information block specified by IEEE Std 1394a-2000 and a unit directory specified by this document.

The max_rec field in its bus information block MUST be at least 8, which indicates an ability to accept block write requests and asynchronous stream packets with a data payload of 512 octets. The same ability MUST also apply to read requests, so the node MUST be able to transmit a block response packet with a data payload of 512 octets.

The node MUST be isochronous resource manager capable, as specified by IEEE Std 1394a-2000, and MUST support both reception and transmission of asynchronous streams as specified by that standard.
sections.plainLanguage: A device on the bus has to be able to carry 512-byte payloads both ways, and has to be able to manage the timed streams that the bus uses for audio and video. In practice this is a requirement on the hardware and its firmware.

sections.title: Encapsulation, Fragmentation and the MTU
sections.content:
The encapsulation and fragmentation mechanism MUST be the same as the link encapsulation and fragmentation section of the IPv4 over IEEE 1394 specification. Since there is an ether_type field to discriminate protocols and MCAP, the multicast channel allocation protocol, is used for both IPv4 and IPv6, the version field in the GASP header of IPv6 datagrams is the same value, one, as in the IPv4 specification. The ether_type value for IPv6 is 0x86dd.

The default MTU size for IPv6 packets on an IEEE 1394 network is 1500 octets. This size may be reduced by a Router Advertisement containing an MTU option which specifies a smaller MTU, or by manual configuration of each node. If a Router Advertisement received on an IEEE 1394 interface has an MTU option specifying an MTU larger than 1500, or larger than a manually configured value, that MTU option may be logged to system management but MUST be otherwise ignored. The mechanism to extend the MTU size between particular two nodes is for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 packets ride in exactly the same kind of 1394 packet as IPv4 ones, and the field that says which protocol is inside holds 0x86dd for IPv6. The largest packet is 1500 bytes by default, and a router can only lower that.

sections.title: Building the Interface Identifier
sections.content:
The Interface Identifier for an IEEE 1394 interface is formed from the interface's built-in EUI-64 identifier by complementing the Universal/Local bit, which is the next-to-lowest order bit of the first octet of the EUI-64 identifier. Complementing this bit will generally change a 0 value to a 1, since an interface's built-in EUI-64 identifier is expected to be from a universally administered address space and hence have a globally unique value. A universally administered EUI-64 identifier is signified by a 0 in the U/L bit position, while a globally unique IPv6 Interface Identifier is signified by a 1 in the corresponding position.

An IPv6 address prefix used for stateless autoconfiguration of an IEEE 1394 interface MUST have a length of 64 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Each 1394 interface has a unique 64-bit identifier built into it. The IPv6 address is built from that, with one bit flipped to say the address is not globally unique, which is the convention for a locally administered address.

sections.title: Link-Local Addresses
sections.content: The IPv6 link-local address for an IEEE 1394 interface is formed by appending the Interface Identifier, as defined above, to the prefix FE80::/64. The address therefore has ten bits of prefix, 54 bits of zeros and the 64-bit interface identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The address that only works on this one bus is the usual FE80:: prefix followed by the interface identifier that was just described.

sections.title: Mapping Addresses for Unicast
sections.content:
The procedure for mapping IPv6 unicast addresses into IEEE 1394 link-layer addresses uses Neighbor Discovery. Since a 1394 link address, the node_ID, will not be constant across a 1394 bridge, it has not been put in the Link-layer Address option. The recipient of the Neighbor Discovery SHOULD use the source_ID, obtained from either the asynchronous packet header or the GASP header, in conjunction with the content of the Source link-layer address. An implementation MAY use some other methods to obtain a node_ID of the sender, utilizing a mapping table between the node_unique_ID and the node_ID; the mechanism to make such a mapping table is out of scope of this document.

The recipient of a Neighbor Discovery packet MUST ignore it unless the most significant ten bits of the source_ID are equal to either 0x3FF or the most significant ten bits of the recipient's NODE_IDS register.

The Source/Target Link-layer Address option has the form shown in the RFC when the link layer is IEEE 1394. The Type field is 1 for a Source Link-layer address and 2 for a Target Link-layer address, and the Length is 3 in units of 8 octets. The node_unique_ID field contains the node unique ID of the node and MUST be equal to that specified in the node's configuration ROM. The max_rec field MUST be equal to the value of max_rec in the node's configuration ROM. The spd field MUST be set to the lesser of the node's link speed and PHY speed. The unicast_FIFO field MUST specify the 48-bit offset of the node's FIFO available for the receipt of IPv6 datagrams, and that offset MUST NOT change except as the result of a power reset. The reserved fields MUST be set to all zeros by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

Note that a node_ID may change when a 1394 bus reset occurs, and the mapping cache held in the node SHOULD be cleared on a bus reset.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbour discovery messages carry the hardware identifier of the sender, because the bus-assigned number is not stable across a bridge. The receiver also checks that the message really came from the same bus, using the top bits of the source identifier, and ignores it otherwise.

sections.title: IPv6 Multicast
sections.content:
By default, all best-effort IPv6 multicast MUST use asynchronous stream packets whose channel number is equal to the channel field from the BROADCAST_CHANNEL register. In particular, datagrams addressed to all-nodes multicast addresses, all-routers multicast addresses, and solicited-node multicast addresses MUST use the default channel specified by the BROADCAST_CHANNEL register.

Best-effort IPv6 multicast for other multicast group addresses may utilize a different channel number if such a channel number is allocated and advertised prior to use, by the multicast channel allocation protocol, MCAP. When a node wishes to receive multicast data addressed to other than the all-nodes, all-routers and solicited-node multicast addresses, it MUST confirm that the channel mapping between a multicast group address and a channel number exists using MCAP.

The implementation of MCAP is optional for send-only nodes. A node MAY transmit multicast data addressed to any multicast address into the default broadcast channel regardless of the existing allocation of the channel. If a node wishes to transmit multicast data on other than the default channel, it MUST first confirm by MCAP whether or not a channel number for the group address has already been allocated. Implementors are encouraged to use this protocol when transmitting high-rate multicast streams. The MCAP type value for the IPv6 group address descriptor is 2.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast traffic goes out on one reserved channel by default. A node that wants to use a different channel for a group has to check with the channel allocation protocol first, so that two streams do not end up on the same channel.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: IPv6 over IEEE 1394 does not introduce any additional security considerations over the IPv4 over IEEE 1394 specification. The security concerns described in that document apply here as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here adds a new security problem: the same considerations that apply to IPv4 on this bus apply to IPv6.
